analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for federal officers to neglect medical care for people in custody showing medical distress.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in the House Judiciary Committee at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime — punishable by up to a year in prison and a fine — for federal law enforcement officers and Bureau of Prisons staff to negligently fail to get immediate medical help for someone in federal custody who shows medical distress, such as breathing trouble. It would also require agency Inspectors General to investigate such incidents, set up a confidential complaint process, and mandate training for officers. It is named for Andrew Kearse, who died in 2017 after repeatedly pleading for medical help while in police custody. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People held in federal custody — federal detainees, prisoners, and people under arrest by federal officers — who are disproportionately poor, and their families. It gives them a criminal remedy, an Inspector General investigation, and a confidential complaint channel when officers ignore obvious medical emergencies.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal offense for a covered official — a federal law enforcement officer or Bureau of Prisons employee — who negligently fails to obtain or provide immediate medical attention to a person in federal custody displaying medical distress, if that failure causes unnecessary pain, injury, or death.
Sets penalties of a fine, up to one year in prison, or both, and defines medical distress to include breathing difficulties.
Requires the relevant Inspector General to investigate every such incident, refer cases for prosecution when negligence is found, and operate a confidential complaint process for reporting officers.

Requires agency heads to train covered officials on getting medical assistance for people in distress, and lets state attorneys general sue in federal court for equitable and declaratory relief on behalf of harmed residents.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies and the Bureau of Prisons, which would face new criminal liability for their officers and staff, plus the cost of mandatory training and Inspector General investigations.

drawbacks.text: The penalty is modest — no more than one year in prison — and the offense requires only negligence, which some would say under-punishes officers who ignore a medical emergency, while others would argue criminal negligence charges could make officers overly cautious or defensive.

The bill covers federal custody only. It would not apply to state or local police or jails, where most people are held — including the circumstances of the case the bill is named for, so it would not have covered that situation.
The state attorney general enforcement route provides only equitable and declaratory relief — a court order or a statement that the law was violated — not money damages for the victim's family.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is narrow but real: it puts a specific, well-defined duty — call for medical help when someone in your custody is in visible medical distress — backed by a modest criminal penalty and mandatory investigation. The main honest criticisms are that one year is a light penalty for a death, and that covering only federal custody leaves out the state and local systems where most people are held. As written, it would have helped a vulnerable population at little public cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2020 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never held a markup or vote on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the bill on June 18, 2020, joined by 17 other House members, all Democrats, as cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and no further action of any kind appears in the record — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement and prison officials are better off because the bill died: they face no new criminal liability for failing to get medical help for people in custody, and the Inspector General investigation and complaint requirements never took effect.

for.name: Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House and recruited 17 cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Jerrold Nadler (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 18, 2020 and never scheduled a markup or committee vote; the bill never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a roll-call vote. Sponsorship was entirely Democratic — one sponsor and 17 cosponsors, all from that party — with no recorded Republican support, but no one ever voted on the bill publicly.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement officers and agencies (including the Bureau of Prisons)
industries.note: Because the bill died, federal officers and prison staff avoid a new one-year criminal penalty and mandatory Inspector General investigations for negligently denying medical care to people in custody. The industry's interest in avoiding accountability ran against the interests of the people they hold.
